topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

fields.definition: A near-field (home/consumer) re-recording of a program's soundtrack adapted for a specific language or territory, in which localized (dubbed) dialogue is combined with the original music-and-effects (M&E) and monitored at near-field/home reference level rather than at theatrical level.
fields.plain_english: This is the home-video version of a show's sound, remade in another language. The new spoken lines are mixed with the original music and sound effects. It is checked on small studio speakers, like the ones people use at home.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a program reach non-original-language home and broadcast audiences by swapping the dialogue while keeping the original musical and effects intent, optimized for consumer near-field playback.
fields.practical_application: A re-recording mixer conforms the home mix by placing the dubbed language stem over the delivered M&E, checks balance and loudness on near-field monitors, and outputs the territory's consumer deliverable.
common_mistakes: Reusing the theatrical mix at home level without adjusting dialogue clarity and dynamics for near-field playback
Failing to check that the localized dialogue sits correctly against the original M&E balance
Delivering at the wrong integrated loudness target for the consumer platform
scenario_contexts: Preparing a French home-video mix of an English feature
Creating a consumer or broadcast version after the theatrical mix is locked
QC of a dubbed near-field deliverable before release

sources: Yewdall, 'Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: A printmaster—the final, fully combined mix rendered to its delivery channel layout—prepared for a localized version of a program, in which the territory's dubbed dialogue is printed together with the original music-and-effects (M&E) stems.
fields.plain_english: A printmaster is the finished, combined soundtrack that gets sent out. A localized one uses new dubbed voices in place of the first language. The music and sound effects stay the same.
fields.purpose_function: It provides the ready-to-encode soundtrack for a specific language so distribution and mastering can proceed without re-opening the full mix session.
fields.practical_application: Once the dubbed dialogue is approved, the mixer prints the combined dialogue and original M&E to the required channel layout, creating the localized printmaster used for encoding and QC.
common_mistakes: Confusing a printmaster (fully combined) with stems (separated elements)
Printing before the dubbed dialogue is fully approved, forcing costly re-prints
Mismatching channel order or LFE routing versus the delivery spec
scenario_contexts: Rendering the German 5.1 printmaster of a series episode
Handing a localized printmaster to mastering for DCP or file encoding
Archiving language-specific printmasters for future re-release

sources: Yewdall, 'Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: A streaming-platform deliverable of a program's mix adapted for a specific language or territory and conformed to that platform's channel-layout and loudness specifications, combining localized (dubbed) dialogue with the original music-and-effects (M&E).
fields.plain_english: This is the sound version made for a streaming service in another language. It follows that service's rules for how loud the sound can be. New voices replace the first language, but the music and effects stay.
fields.purpose_function: It delivers a language-specific mix that meets a streaming platform's technical and loudness requirements so it plays back correctly and consistently across consumer devices.
fields.practical_application: The mixer conforms the dubbed mix to the platform's channel layout and loudness target, measures integrated loudness and true peak, and delivers the file for that territory.
common_mistakes: Missing the platform's integrated loudness or true-peak limits
Assuming one loudness target fits every platform
Not verifying dubbed dialogue intelligibility on small consumer speakers
scenario_contexts: Delivering a Spanish 5.1 mix to a streaming service at its loudness spec
Re-versioning a title for several territories on one platform
QC of true-peak and integrated loudness before upload

fields.definition: A theatrical (cinema) re-recording of a program's soundtrack adapted for a specific language or territory, calibrated to theatrical reference monitoring (about 85 dB SPL per channel with the cinema X-curve response) and combining dubbed dialogue with the original music-and-effects (M&E).
fields.plain_english: This is the movie-theater version of the sound, redone in another language. It is set up to be loud and full for a big cinema room. New spoken lines sit over the original music and sound effects.
fields.purpose_function: It recreates the cinema soundtrack in another language at theatrical standards so foreign-market audiences get the intended large-room presentation.
fields.practical_application: On a calibrated dubbing stage, the mixer places dubbed dialogue over the original M&E and prints the localized theatrical version for DCP mastering.
common_mistakes: Mixing a theatrical-bound dub on near-field monitors instead of a calibrated stage
Ignoring the X-curve and theatrical reference level when judging brightness and level
Letting dubbed dialogue drift away from the original balance
scenario_contexts: Producing the Italian theatrical dub of a feature for cinema release
Re-recording localized dialogue on a calibrated dubbing stage
Delivering a localized DCP audio master

sources: Yewdall, 'Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: The complete set of audio deliverables assembled to release a program in a specific language or territory—typically the localized final mixes and printmasters, the music-and-effects (M&E) and stems, and the accompanying metadata and QC/configuration documentation.
fields.plain_english: This is the full set of sound files sent out for one language or country. It holds the finished mixes, the music-and-effects track, and notes about each file. Studios use it so a show can be released in that place.
fields.purpose_function: It bundles everything a distributor needs for one territory so the correct mixes, source stems, and documentation travel together and match the client's spec.
fields.practical_application: A post supervisor assembles the localized printmasters/mixes, M&E, stems, and metadata into one organized package that conforms to the delivery specification.
common_mistakes: Omitting the M&E or a required stem set from the package
Inconsistent file naming or metadata versus the delivery spec
Delivering the wrong channel layout or loudness variant for the territory
scenario_contexts: Compiling the French-territory audio package for a distributor
Cross-checking a localized package against a studio delivery spec
Archiving a per-territory package for later re-versioning

sources: Yewdall, 'Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: A recorded ADR (automated dialogue replacement, historically called 'looping') element—an individual replacement line or a loop-group recording—delivered as a discrete, reusable media asset for dialogue editing and the final mix.
fields.plain_english: Looping is when actors re-record their lines in a quiet studio. It is also called ADR. A looping asset is one of those recorded lines, saved as a file for the mix.
fields.purpose_function: It supplies clean, controlled replacement dialogue to fix unusable production sound or add lines, giving editors and mixers reusable material.
fields.practical_application: A dialogue editor imports the ADR or loop-group recordings, syncs each line to picture, and hands the assets to the re-recording mixer for the dialogue stem.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'looping' and 'ADR' are different processes—they are the same
Poor sync or mismatched room tone between the looping asset and the scene
Not labeling assets by character and line, which slows the edit
scenario_contexts: Replacing a noisy on-set line with an ADR looping asset
Adding loop-group crowd walla to a stadium scene
Delivering character ADR takes to the dialogue editor

sources: Yewdall, 'Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'

fields.definition: The dedicated, band-limited low-frequency channel in a surround deliverable—the '.1' of formats such as 5.1 and 7.1—designated LFE (Low-Frequency Effects in film; also expanded 'low frequency enhancement' in ITU domestic-system terminology), carrying high-level low-frequency content of roughly 20–120 Hz reproduced by the subwoofer.
fields.plain_english: This is the deep-bass channel in surround sound, the '.1' in 5.1. It carries the low rumble you feel, like explosions or thunder. A subwoofer plays it.
fields.purpose_function: It carries high-level, band-limited bass on its own channel so the main channels are not overdriven and impactful low-frequency content is reproduced by a subwoofer.
fields.practical_application: The mixer routes and meters LFE content within the format's band limit and level standard, and confirms bass management and channel order match the delivery spec.
common_mistakes: Confusing the LFE (.1) channel with full-range low bass in the main channels
Overloading LFE and exceeding the format's headroom and level standard
Wrong channel-order mapping so LFE lands on the wrong track
scenario_contexts: Setting LFE level and low-pass for a 5.1 printmaster
Checking bass management on the monitoring system
Verifying LFE routing against a delivery channel map

fields.definition: A calibrated, acoustically controlled listening room used to audition and quality-check finished masters and deliverables before release, with monitoring level and response aligned to the applicable delivery standard so evaluations are consistent and repeatable.
fields.plain_english: This is a carefully set-up listening room. A team plays the finished sound here to check it before it ships. The speakers and volume are tuned to a set standard so everyone hears it the same way.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a trusted, standardized listening environment so finished masters can be evaluated and approved with consistent, repeatable results.
fields.practical_application: QC and mastering staff play back deliverables at calibrated level and response to catch loudness, sync, dropout, and channel errors before sign-off.
common_mistakes: Judging masters on uncalibrated speakers or at an inconsistent level
Skipping full-length playback and missing dropouts or sync errors
UNSAFE: Reviewing for long stretches at high SPL without breaks, risking noise-induced hearing loss (observe OSHA 1910.95 exposure limits)
scenario_contexts: Final QC of a feature's printmaster before delivery
Comparing localized versions for level and balance consistency
Signing off a master after calibrated playback

fields.definition: Foley footstep performances (or selected library steps) chosen and executed to match the surface material a character walks on—for example wood, concrete, gravel, grass, or metal—so the step sounds correspond to the on-screen ground.
fields.plain_english: These are footstep sounds picked to match the ground on screen. A wood floor, gravel, and grass each sound different. Foley artists walk on the right surface so the steps fit the picture.
fields.purpose_function: It makes footsteps believable by matching their timbre to the on-screen surface, reinforcing realism and a character's presence in the space.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist selects the right shoe and walks the performance on a matching surface pit (wood, concrete, gravel, and so on), recorded in sync to picture for the Foley/effects stem.
common_mistakes: Using one generic footstep sound regardless of the surface on screen
Mismatched shoe or surface so the steps read as fake
Poor sync between the step performance and the picture
scenario_contexts: Performing gravel footsteps for an exterior walking scene
Building a Foley footstep pass across changing surfaces
Delivering material-matched footsteps in the Foley stem for the M&E

sources: Yewdall, 'Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound'
